hints: Look closely at the word always. Think about what the active site actually is: a precise 3D pocket made from amino acids that may be far apart in the chain.
Ask yourself which levels every single enzyme must have to make that 3D pocket, and which level only exists in enzymes made of more than one polypeptide.
walkthrough:
**Picture what an active site needs**

Think of the active site as a tiny, perfectly shaped pocket. Its shape depends on exactly which amino acids are present and exactly how the chain is folded in 3D.

That already points us to sequence and folding.

**Check primary and tertiary structure**

Primary structure is the sequence of amino acids. This always matters, because it decides which R groups can form the active site.

Tertiary structure is the further folding into a precise 3D shape. This always matters too, because folding brings distant amino acids together to make the pocket.

**Check quaternary structure**

Quaternary structure means two or more polypeptides joined together. Many enzymes have only one polypeptide, so they have no quaternary structure at all.

Therefore quaternary cannot be always involved. Primary and tertiary are always involved, which matches option B.

options.A: Primary and tertiary are correct, but quaternary is not always involved because many enzymes are made of a single polypeptide.
options.B: Primary is always involved as the amino acid sequence, and tertiary is always involved as the 3D folding that creates the active site. Quaternary is correctly excluded.
options.C: Tertiary is correct, but primary should be ticked and quaternary should not be ticked, so this combination is wrong.
options.D: Quaternary alone is wrong because single-polypeptide enzymes have no quaternary structure, while primary and tertiary are both essential for every active site.
